title: R’ Yitzchak Paskaa
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman calls him a great man of R’ Yochanan’s time. Eichah Rabbah 1:37 relates that when R’ Yose of Mamlachya died, R’ Yochanan and Resh Lakish went up, with R’ Yitzchak Paskaa. An elder wished to eulogize him, but Yitzchak Paskaa stopped him: “Arise! These are lions, and you open your mouth?” R’ Yochanan allowed him to speak. At the end, Yitzchak Paskaa said: “May this man’s mouth be blessed.” R’ Yochanan replied: “Had you not let him speak, we would not have heard this.”

notes.text: The supplied שט appears where the checked text reads “there.” It remains a source anomaly. The checked passage explicitly distinguishes Yohanan from Yitzchak Paskaa and supports the latter as the one initially objecting to the elder.

No new primary scalar was returned. The surname Paskaa locally distinguishes Yitzchak from Yochanan, removing the older invented alternation over the initial objector and final blesser. The earlier Eichah comparison is inherited, not newly inspected. Supplied שט is read contextually as there beside possible שם, without claiming a tet/mem transcription history. The imperative ARISE is restored, and the closing counterfactual is preserved as supplied. Hyman calls him a great man of Yochanan’s time; this is an attributed characterization, not a separately dated biography. All uninspected abbreviated title components remain R’.

The consulted Eichah Rabbah 1:37 says there was an elder there and distinguishes the parties: the first refusal is in the plural, Yitzchak addresses the elder and later blesses him, and Yochanan tells the group to let him speak. It reads “Before these lions of Torah.” The Hebrew uses a plural form in the closing counterfactual and calls what they heard a pearl, while the edition’s English gives “Had we not allowed him.” Hyman’s printed account has the imperative קום, shortens the eulogy, and gives the closing counterfactual as translated in the body.
